target.title: Lightweight Diffusion-based Framework for Online Imagined Speech Decoding in Aphasia

entries.text: The authors characterize existing imagined-speech decoding as predominantly offline or computationally demanding; the paper provides no head-to-head comparison establishing superiority.
entries.condition: Literature framing in the abstract; no comparative baseline is reported in this paper.

entries.text: The paradigm is a four-class Korean-language task: three participant-selected imagined-speech targets tied to daily communication plus resting state; the printed English glosses are Clock, Toilet, and Water.
entries.condition: One participant; imagined-speech targets selected around daily communicative needs and a resting-state class.

questions.q: What does the paper demonstrate empirically about online decoding, and under what conditions?
questions.answer: It reports 65% top-1 and 70% top-2 accuracy in a single participant's four-class, 20-trial online feedback session lasting approximately 5 minutes; Water was 80%/100%. The result is a one-participant feasibility demonstration, not evidence of cross-participant performance.

questions.q: Does the study establish that its decoder is superior to prior approaches?
questions.answer: No head-to-head baseline or ablation is reported. The paper frames prior work as predominantly offline or computationally demanding and presents the online result as feasibility evidence; comparative superiority remains untested.

questions.q: Which evaluation conditions are missing for interpreting or reproducing the reported accuracy?
questions.answer: The paper omits online per-class trial counts, seeds/repeated runs, independent participant testing, train/validation split details, additional feature normalization, a chance-level reference, and language-model/lexical-aid details.

questions.q: What limitations do the authors themselves acknowledge?
questions.answer: They identify the pilot cohort's limited generalizability, the need for subject-specific calibration, and the restriction to a four-class vocabulary, and propose more participants, transfer/adaptive fine-tuning, and vocabulary expansion.

questions.q: Can the overall row of Table I (65% top-1, 70% top-2) be derived from the per-class rows?
questions.answer: No. Per-class top-2 minus top-1 gains are 20, 60, 20 and 20 points; any allocation of the 20 trials gives an overall gain of at least 20 points, but the overall row shows 5. With 5 trials per class the per-class rows give 50% top-1 and 80% top-2. Per-class trial counts are not reported (t44) and confusion matrices are computed but not shown (t61).

questions.q: Does Diff-E run reverse diffusion sampling at test time, and how large is it?
questions.answer: No: only the encoder and classifier are used at inference (c1); DDPM plus CAE about 300,000 parameters and classifier 400,000 (c2). The multi-kernel ensemble also classifies without sampling (c8).
